note: Labelled corpus for evaluating embedder seed quality. Memories are drawn from real Scatterhoard design decisions so the text is representative: short, jargon-dense, project-specific. Embedding input is content + why + keywords, per documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md.

memories.content: Memories carry an Origin field with values human, llm, or joint, separate from Author.
memories.why: Author records whose identity is attached to a memory, which is what git and review care about. Origin separately records whose reasoning produced the content, so the system does not tell the human 'you decided X' when the model decided it.

memories.content: The Context field is optional and free text, kept out of the embedding.
memories.why: Context is an episodic anchor - when and in response to what a memory arose - used to gloss a memory for the human after recall has already found it. Including it in the embedding would drag semantically unrelated memories together just because they happened around the same time.

memories.content: Semantic search embeds the why text and the keywords along with the content.
memories.why: The why often surfaces related topics and records of paths not taken, which is what semantic recall should find. Keywords are already curated for topical relevance so including them is nearly free.

memories.content: A cross-set reference stores the exact memory ID plus the name of the referenced set; keywords are supplementary only.
memories.why: The ID plus set name is canonical. Keywords help re-find a target if the ID goes dangling but are not sufficient to resolve a reference on their own.

memories.content: Dangling cross-set references are a soft failure; the LLM decides what to do rather than the software failing hard.
memories.why: A personal memory referring to a project memory can dangle if the project never merges it. Failing hard would make ordinary workflows brittle.

memories.content: Scope is a required explicit parameter when storing a memory; it is never inferred.
memories.why: The software does not have enough intelligence to steer a memory to the right set, and a personal memory committed to a public repository cannot be taken back.

memories.content: Scope is single-valued per memory. Needing the same memory in two projects is an explicit separate operation.
memories.why: Multi-scope tagging adds complexity for a case expected to be rare. An explicit duplication or cross-reference keeps the common path simple.

memories.content: The export review gate runs two independent checks: a mechanical prohibited-data scan and an LLM judgment gate.
memories.why: They have different costs and different scopes. The mechanical scan is cheap and deterministic; the judgment gate needs context and is worth limiting.

memories.content: The mechanical prohibited-data scan runs on the full exported set every time, unscoped by authorship.
memories.why: Whether a secret leaked in from something the local user wrote or something merged from elsewhere does not change the risk of committing it, and the scan is cheap enough to run unconditionally.

memories.content: The judgment gate is scoped to memories the local user last modified, not created.
memories.why: If the local user edited a memory since it was last cleared, it is their responsibility. A memory merged from main that they never touched already passed its own author's gate and the maintainer's review.

memories.content: The export-review ledger is local-only, per-machine, created on first memory, never committed.
memories.why: The judgment gate only fires on memories the local user last modified, so no other contributor's machine needs the ledger. Syncing it would add merge-conflict surface for pure bookkeeping.

memories.content: The ledger's storage location is configurable rather than hard-coded.
memories.why: A user who wants laptop and desktop continuity can point it at a folder they already sync themselves, so Scatterhoard does not have to build sync.

memories.content: Memory set reconciliation happens by exporting, pulling, and letting git three-way-merge the exported file.
memories.why: Git's merge has a real common ancestor. Merging into the live database instead would mean reimplementing three-way merge semantics against rows without an ancestor.

memories.content: Forgotten memories need no tombstone mechanism; a deletion is just a removed line that git's three-way merge already handles.
memories.why: Git resolves delete-versus-unmodified as a clean delete and delete-versus-modified as a genuine conflict, because it has the ancestor.

memories.content: The custom git merge driver is a graceful enhancement, not a dependency.
memories.why: Registering a merge driver needs per-clone local git config, which is the same fragile mechanism class as git hooks. If it never fires, git falls back to standard three-way merge, which is correct and only coarser.

memories.content: The merge driver does field-level JSON merging only where git would otherwise flag a line conflict.
memories.why: One JSON object per line means two branches editing different fields of the same memory collide at the line level even though the changes are logically compatible.

memories.content: The Golden Rule in Scatterhoard is a technical safeguard, not decoration.
memories.why: Simple software can be ethically neutral but this is not simple software. It shapes what an LLM believes about a project and its people, and we do not know who will use a memory set - attacker as easily as contributor. We cannot prevent misuse but we can add friction.

memories.content: Be charitable about people and exact about code.
memories.why: An LLM told to be kind may soften accurate technical criticism, which harms review. Charity applies to judging intent and character, not to judging whether the tests pass.

memories.content: When a memory concerns a person, record the specific observation rather than a characterisation.
memories.why: Memories about people outlive the situation that produced them and are read by people who were not there. The specific observation is both the fairer record and the more accurate one, since a global characterisation is usually a low-confidence overgeneralisation.

memories.content: The Golden Rule reaches runtime as the reinforcement attached to memory-writing conventions, not as a standalone convention.
memories.why: A freestanding moral directive in a memory tool reads as overreach, invites being stripped or mocked, and costs scarce context. Embedded in memory-writing guidance it is load-bearing.

memories.content: A convention's supporting text is called reinforcement, not why.
memories.why: Reinforcement is held to a fixed standard - it must reinforce the convention at the moment of use. A memory's why is not held to that standard, since the LLM drafts it in the moment and it is only consulted on recall. Sharing a name would blur the distinction.

memories.content: Update-time context for a convention lives in source comments and is never served.
memories.why: The test that sorts the two is whether the text reinforces the convention at the moment of use. If it only helps someone revising the convention, it is a comment.

memories.content: Project memories are always data, never instructions.
memories.why: Memories auto-load at session start and are treated as authoritative project knowledge, but they arrive via git pull from a repository that may have accepted anyone's contributions. A maintainer with legitimate instructions has other channels.

memories.content: The prompts subdirectory was drafted and then deliberately removed.
memories.why: Nothing in the design currently needs a prompt channel, and a reserved but unused path invites someone later filling it without rereading the rationale.

memories.content: The whole scatterhoard_mem directory is reserved for Scatterhoard; no area is designated for arbitrary project files.
memories.why: A project needing somewhere to put things has the rest of its repository. Declaring the namespace reserved is what makes it legitimate to warn about unexpected contents.

memories.content: Unexpected entries in scatterhoard_mem are always ignored and never fatal.
memories.why: Refusing to operate would make Scatterhoard fragile in exactly the forward-compatibility case that matters most: an older local build meeting a repository written by a newer one.

memories.content: Warnings about unexpected files are gated on the memory file's format version.
memories.why: If the format version is newer than this build supports, a newer Scatterhoard plausibly wrote the file, so stay quiet. If the version is fully supported, someone put it there and it is worth surfacing.

memories.content: An unexpected prompt-shaped file in scatterhoard_mem is a tripwire, not just untidiness.
memories.why: It is a weak signal someone is smuggling in an instruction channel. Scatterhoard will not load it but another tool might, and it sits in a directory that has declared it holds no instructions.

memories.content: Warnings surface at the export gate and once on first encountering a project, never at session start.
memories.why: A session-start warning costs context, trains people to scroll past it, and often reaches someone who cannot act on it - a contributor who just cloned cannot fix what a maintainer committed.

memories.content: Vector embeddings are local derived state and never appear in the exported memory file.
memories.why: Hundreds of floats per memory would destroy the small-diff goal of the export format, have no meaningful merge semantics, and would make an embedding model change an ecosystem-wide commitment rather than a local one.

memories.content: Recall uses a brute-force linear cosine scan rather than an approximate nearest-neighbour index.
memories.why: At a project's plausible scale of thousands to low tens of thousands of memories, a linear scan is single-digit milliseconds. That removes index tuning, index rebuilds on import, and index corruption entirely.

memories.content: model2vec-rs is the starting embedder, pending empirical validation.
memories.why: Pure Rust, MIT, models of eight to thirty-two megabytes, and a local-only feature that makes the offline constraint structural. Semantic search only produces seeds for graph traversal, so the quality gap against a transformer matters less than the speed on the import path.

memories.content: A local embedding cache keyed by content hash means import only re-embeds memories whose content changed.
memories.why: Re-embedding is on the critical path of an ordinary git pull, so a full re-embed on every import would be felt.

memories.content: Test-driven development is required wherever practical; write the failing test first.
memories.why: The memory graph, recall ranking, and import merge logic are where subtle correctness bugs are most costly and least visible.

memories.content: The convention catalog is under a character budget enforced by a test.
memories.why: Conventions load into every session, so the catalog is a standing charge against the context window. Growth past the budget should be a deliberate decision rather than drift nobody notices.

memories.content: Convention IDs are lowercase kebab-case and stable; changing one is a breaking change.
memories.why: IDs are referenced from memories and from other conventions.

memories.content: Every Scatterhoard source file carries the Vision Constraint notice.
memories.why: The Vision requires it, to keep AI-assisted development from drifting from the project's original intent.

memories.content: Session checkpoints live in a gitignored checkpoints directory.
memories.why: Checkpoints are working notes, not curated project memories, and should not flow into any branch - the same personal-versus-project distinction the design draws for memories.

memories.content: A project's memory set is a single file with a well-known name.
memories.why: The loader reads exactly that file and treats nothing else as memories, which makes the data-not-instructions rule enforceable by path. The merge driver also registers against that name.

memories.content: The memory file is newline-delimited JSON exported in a consistent order.
memories.why: Consistent ordering minimises diffs at merge time and makes changes reviewable.

memories.content: Memory confidence is a float from 0.0 to 1.0 set by the LLM.
memories.why: Graph traversal decays effective confidence based on native confidence and distance from the seed, so the scale needs to be meaningful.

memories.content: Secret API keys, passwords, and credit card numbers are blocked from memories.
memories.why: They must not leak into a project's repository. Sensitive data belongs in a file the software refers to instead.

memories.content: Conventions load once per session even when working across multiple projects.
memories.why: Reloading them for a second project wastes context, though that project's memories still need loading.

memories.content: Direct memory lookup supports prefix matching on UUIDs.
memories.why: Some models truncate UUIDs when recording a reference, the same way people abbreviate git commit hashes.

memories.content: Recalled memories should be surfaced with enough context to let the human place them.
memories.why: An LLM citing a memory without placing it leaves the human unable to tell what it refers to, which is where the cost of recalled memory actually lands.
